course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

topic.title: Native American Societies Before European Contact
topic.summary: How maize, aridity, mixed farming, and ocean resources shaped the economies and settlements of Native American societies across North America before 1491.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was an effect of the spread of maize cultivation into the present-day American Southwest?
choices: Irrigated farming supported larger settlements, and the region's peoples united under one centralized empire
Farmers abandoned permanent settlements so that they could follow bison herds across the grasslands
Irrigated farming supported larger permanent settlements and greater social diversification
Farming ended the need for trade because each village could grow every resource it needed
questions.explanation: Where maize spread and could be irrigated, harvests grew, and societies built permanent settlements and developed specialized roles.
choiceExplanations: Farming did support larger settlements, but Southwest societies stayed politically separate.
Maize farming encouraged settlement; following bison was a Plains way of life.
Where maize spread and could be irrigated, harvests grew, and societies built permanent settlements and developed specialized roles.
Southwest societies took part in trade networks, and surplus food supported traders.
questions.distinguisher: Maize did support larger settlements, but the Hohokam and Pueblo peoples remained separate societies rather than one empire.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why many Native societies in the Great Basin developed largely mobile lifestyles?
choices: The region's aridity limited farming, so groups moved seasonally to gather scarce food
Huge herds of bison covered the region's grasslands, so hunters followed the herds across long distances
Frequent flooding of the region's rivers destroyed villages, so families moved to higher ground each year
Spanish explorers forced these communities to move away from the coast and into the interior
questions.explanation: Aridity in the Great Basin meant little farmland, so people moved with the seasons to find seeds, nuts, and small game.
choiceExplanations: Aridity in the Great Basin meant little farmland, so people moved with the seasons to find seeds, nuts, and small game.
Bison herds shaped mobility on the Great Plains, but the Great Basin was dry and had few large herds.
The Great Basin was dry, not flood-prone, and its rivers did not drive repeated relocation.
These mobile lifestyles developed before European contact.
questions.distinguisher: Mobility on the Plains came from following bison; in the Great Basin it came from aridity and scattered food.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the economies of many Native societies in the Northeast and along the Atlantic seaboard before 1491?
choices: Large-scale irrigated agriculture that supported crowded cities governed by a single ruler
Hunting and gathering only, with no use of crops and few lasting settlements in any season
Trade in ocean products such as salmon and whale oil, which replaced local farming entirely
A mix of farming with hunting, fishing, and gathering that supported permanent villages near fields
questions.explanation: Many eastern peoples combined farming with hunting, fishing, and gathering, and their food supply supported permanent villages.
choiceExplanations: Large irrigated farms were characteristic of the Southwest, not of the East.
Many eastern peoples grew maize, beans, and squash and kept permanent villages.
Salmon and whaling belong to the Pacific Northwest, and eastern societies farmed.
Many eastern peoples combined farming with hunting, fishing, and gathering, and their food supply supported permanent villages.
questions.distinguisher: Irrigated agriculture was important in the Southwest, but eastern societies relied on rainfall-based farming mixed with hunting.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains how many Eastern Woodlands societies could live in permanent villages while still hunting and fishing?
choices: Trade with Spanish colonists provided steady food, so hunting was no longer necessary for survival
Farming provided a dependable food supply, and seasonal hunting and fishing added to it
Hunting supplied almost all food, and villages were occupied only briefly each year during the winter
Irrigation canals watered large fields, which freed families from the need to fish or hunt at all
questions.explanation: Crops such as maize, beans, and squash gave a reliable base, and seasonal hunting and fishing supplemented it.
choiceExplanations: This took place before European contact, so trade with colonists cannot explain it.
Crops such as maize, beans, and squash gave a reliable base, and seasonal hunting and fishing supplemented it.
Villages were permanent, and farming supplied a large share of food.
Irrigation canals were a Southwest development, and eastern peoples still hunted and fished.
questions.distinguisher: Both explanations mention hunting, but only the correct one explains permanent villages through reliable farming that began before contact.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Settled communities developed in the Pacific Northwest primarily because
choices: irrigation canals carried river water to large fields of maize that fed growing populations
Spanish missions introduced herding and farming, which ended the need for seasonal movement
abundant salmon, shellfish, and other ocean and river resources provided a reliable food supply
bison herds moved through the region each year, which allowed hunters to build permanent camps
questions.explanation: Reliable ocean and river resources let people settle in villages without farming.
choiceExplanations: Irrigated maize farming belongs to the Southwest; Northwest peoples did not rely on maize.
Settled communities existed there before Spanish missions.
Reliable ocean and river resources let people settle in villages without farming.
Bison were a resource of the Great Plains, not of the Pacific coast.
questions.distinguisher: Irrigated maize also supported settlement, but in the Southwest; the Northwest relied on salmon and the ocean.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: A comparison of the Southwest with the Great Basin before 1491 best supports which of the following conclusions?
choices: Climate alone determined political organization, so societies in similar environments had identical governments
Different environments led Native societies to develop different economies and settlement patterns
Societies that farmed maize were more advanced than societies that relied on gathering and hunting
All Native societies changed from mobile to settled life as farming spread north from Mexico
questions.explanation: The Southwest supported irrigation and settlement, while the Great Basin's dryness supported mobile gathering, showing that environment shaped economic choices.
choiceExplanations: Environment shaped economies and settlement, but it did not dictate political systems.
The Southwest supported irrigation and settlement, while the Great Basin's dryness supported mobile gathering, showing that environment shaped economic choices.
Mobile societies adapted successfully to their environments; the evidence does not rank them as less advanced.
Farming did not suit every environment, and many societies stayed mobile.
questions.distinguisher: Environment did shape each society, but that does not mean it fixed their governments or ranked their levels of development.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following developments is most relevant context for the growth of the Mississippian city of Cahokia?
choices: The arrival of horses with Spanish explorers, which allowed hunters to follow bison over long distances
The Columbian Exchange, which brought new crops and animals that increased food supplies
The founding of English colonies on the Atlantic coast, which created a demand for trade goods
The spread of maize cultivation, which supported denser populations and permanent settlements
questions.explanation: Maize agriculture gave Mississippian farmers the surplus needed to build and sustain large towns and mounds.
choiceExplanations: Horses arrived with Europeans, after Cahokia had declined.
The Columbian Exchange began in 1492 and came after Cahokia's peak.
English colonies began well after Cahokia was in decline.
Maize agriculture gave Mississippian farmers the surplus needed to build and sustain large towns and mounds.
questions.distinguisher: The other choices name real developments but all came after Cahokia's height, so only maize cultivation is context from before.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a similarity between Native societies of the Pacific Northwest and those of the Eastern Woodlands?
choices: Both developed permanent villages, although they relied on different sources of food
Both relied on maize as the main food source and supported their villages through irrigation canals
Both lived as small mobile groups that traveled with the seasons and avoided building permanent homes
Both were governed by a single confederation that coordinated trade between the two regions
questions.explanation: Northwest peoples settled around ocean and river resources, and eastern peoples around farming, but each lived in permanent villages.
choiceExplanations: Northwest peoples settled around ocean and river resources, and eastern peoples around farming, but each lived in permanent villages.
Northwest peoples did not rely on maize, and eastern farmers did not use large irrigation canals.
Both regions had permanent villages, which is the key similarity.
No such confederation joined the two regions.
questions.distinguisher: The two regions shared permanent villages but not a diet; the maize-and-irrigation choice mistakes eastern farming for Southwest farming and ignores salmon.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Native societies in North America shared one way of life based on farming, which spread from Mexico to every region
Native societies in North America relied only on hunting and gathering until Europeans introduced farming to them
Native societies in North America developed varied ways of life by adapting to, and also changing, their environments
Native societies in North America changed little over time because they adjusted to their surroundings without altering them
questions.explanation: The passage describes different regional societies and then says they also reshaped their environments.
choiceExplanations: The passage describes regional differences, including mobile and coastal societies that did not rely on farming.
The passage describes farming in several regions before 1491.
The passage describes different regional societies and then says they also reshaped their environments.
The passage says Native peoples also reshaped their environments.
questions.distinguisher: The near miss treats maize farming as a single shared pattern, but the passage stresses variety.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 1.2, KC-1.1.I: Different native societies adapted to and transformed their environments through innovations in agriculture, resource use, and social structure
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing how historians describe Native American societies before European contact
stimulusBlocks.text:
Before 1491, Native peoples across North America lived in societies shaped by the land they used. In the Southwest, the spread of maize from present-day Mexico supported farming villages, irrigation, and growing differences in social roles. On the Great Plains and in the Great Basin, where water was scarce, many groups moved with the seasons to hunt, gather, and trade. In the Northeast and the Mississippi River Valley, societies combined farming with hunting and gathering and built permanent villages. Along the Pacific Northwest coast, communities lived well on fish and other resources of the ocean without relying on farming.

Historians note that these societies did more than adjust to their surroundings. Farmers cleared and burned land, built irrigation systems, and carried crops from one region to another, so Native peoples also reshaped their environments.

questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a claim and/or argument in a text-based or non-text-based source.

questions.prompt: Which detail from the passage best supports the claim that Native peoples transformed their environments?
choices: Farmers cleared and burned land, built irrigation systems, and carried crops from one region to another
Societies in the Northeast and the Mississippi River Valley combined farming with hunting and gathering and built permanent villages
Groups on the Great Plains and in the Great Basin moved with the seasons to hunt, gather, and trade
Communities along the Pacific Northwest coast lived well on fish and other resources of the ocean
questions.explanation: Clearing and burning land, building irrigation systems, and moving crops are changes Native peoples made to their surroundings.
choiceExplanations: Clearing and burning land, building irrigation systems, and moving crops are changes Native peoples made to their surroundings.
This shows how those societies made a living and settled; it does not describe changes they made to the land.
This is an example of adapting to a dry environment, not of changing it.
This is an example of using the environment, not of changing it.
questions.distinguisher: Permanent villages show settled life, but only the clearing, burning, and irrigation described in the last sentence show changes to the land itself.

questions.prompt: Which of the following developments most directly made possible the farming villages and irrigation described for the Southwest?
choices: The adoption of the horse, which let groups hunt bison across wide areas of the Plains
The spread of maize cultivation northward from present-day Mexico into the American Southwest
The arrival of Spanish settlers who introduced wheat and livestock to the region
The growth of fishing communities along the Pacific Northwest coast, which supplied the Southwest with food
questions.explanation: The passage says maize spread from present-day Mexico and supported farming villages and irrigation in the Southwest.
choiceExplanations: The horse reached Native peoples after 1492, and it affected the Plains, not Southwest farming.
The passage says maize spread from present-day Mexico and supported farming villages and irrigation in the Southwest.
Southwest farming and irrigation began long before Spanish settlers arrived.
The passage describes the Pacific Northwest as a separate region that did not rely on farming.
questions.distinguisher: The horse transformed some Native societies, but it arrived after contact and did not cause Southwest farming.
